div.p: In this study, we propose simple test statistics for identifying the source of spatial dependence in spatial autoregressive models with endogenous weights matrices. Elements of the weights matrices are modelled in such a way that endogenity arises when the unobserved factors that affect elements of the weights matrices are correlated with the unobserved factors in the outcome equation. The proposed test statistics are robust to the presence of endogeneity in the weights and can be used to detect spatial dependence in the dependent variable and/or the disturbance terms. The robust test statistics are easy to calculate as computationally simple estimations are needed for their calculations. Our Monte Carlo results indicate that these tests have good size and power properties in finite samples. We also provide an empirical illustration to demonstrate the usefulness of the robust tests in identifying the source of spatial dependence.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In spatial and social interaction models, spatial weights matrices (also known as adjacency matrices or network matrices) are used to represent interactions among spatial units in the relevant space. Endogeneity in the weights matrices can arise when the unobserved factors that affect elements of the weights matrices are correlated with the unobserved factors in the outcome equation. For example, in a social interaction model of scholarly achievement, unobserved characteristics such as substance use, psychological disorders and special tutoring, that affect scholarly achievement, may also be associated with the decisions to establish friendships links (Weinberg 2007;Goldsmith-Pinkham and Imbens 2013;Hsieh and Lee 2016). Moreover, three common features observed from survey data on social networks, namely homophily, transitivity of relations and clustering, indicate that individuals with similar characteristics are more likely to form links (Wasserman and Faust 1994;Jackson 2010). Therefore, endogeneity in the spatial weights matrices may arise as these common characteristics could be correlated with the outcome of interest.

Elements of a spatial weights matrix are generally specified using some measure of economic/socioeconomic distance. For example, Case, Rosen, and Hines (1993) study state and local government spendings in the US using a spatial weights matrix whose elements are based on racial composition measured by differences in the percentage of black population. They show evidence for the interdependence in neighbors' expenditures. Brueckner (1998) and Brueckner and Saavedra (2001) construct weights matrices based on relative size of the population to study strategic interactions among local governments. Behrens, Ertur, and Koch (2012) derive a gravity equation from a quantity-based version of the constant elasticity of substitution model to study dependence in trade flows. Conveniently, their theoretical model yields a spatial weights matrix whose elements consist of labor shares of regions.

In the literature, several estimation and testing methods have been introduced for various spatial and social interaction models under the assumption of exogenous weights matrices (Moran 1950;Cliff and Ord 1972;Burridge 1980;Anselin 1988;Anselin et al. 1996;Yang 2015;Baltagi and Li 2001;LeSage and Pace 2009;Lee 2004;Robinson 2008;Kelejian and Prucha 2010;Elhorst 2010;Born and Breitung 2011;Elhorst 2014;Robinson andRossi 2015a, 2014;2015b;Yu, de Jong, and fei Lee 2008;Lee and Yu 2010;Baltagi andYang 2013b, 2013a;Su and Yang 2015;Taşpınar, Doğan, and Vijverberg 2016;Taşpınar, Doğan, and Bera 2017). In the presence of endogenous weights matrices, the conventional estimation and testing methods developed within the generalized method of moments (GMM) and the maximum likelihood (ML) frameworks produce inconsistent estimators and thus lead to incorrect inference.

Recently, Qu and Lee (2015), Qu, Wang, and Lee (2016), and Qu, fei Lee, and Yu (2017) extend the conventional estimation methods to spatial models with endogenous weights matrices using a uniform law of large numbers (ULLN) and a central limit theorem (CLT) developed by Jenish and Prucha (2012) for the near epoch dependent (NED) processes. In these studies, the data generating process (DGP) for the elements of the spatial weights matrix is assumed to be known. Therefore, the model specification consists of two equations where the first equation specifies the spatial autoregressive model, while the second equation specifies how the elements of the spatial weights matrix are generated. In this modeling approach, the endogeneity in weights arises when the error terms of the two equations are correlated. Conventional estimation methods such as ML, GMM and instrumental variable (IV) methods can be used in estimation, since the parametric specification defined for the elements of the weight matrix is used as a control function to account for the endogeneity.

In this paper, we consider a spatial autoregressive model that has spatial dependence in the dependent variable and the disturbance terms, which is an extended version of the model considered by Qu and Lee (2015). We consider the ML estimator (MLE) for the estimation and show its consistency and asymptotic normality in the context of our extended model. Moreover, we develop robust Lagrange multiplier (LM) test statistics for spatial dependence in the dependent variable and/or the disturbance terms. The adjustment in our test statistic is similar to the method developed in Bera et al. (2017) and Bera and Yoon (1993) for parametrically misspecified alternative models. The control function approach, that accounts for the endogeneity in the spatial weights in the estimation, also allows us to formulate test statistics that are robust to the presence of endogeneity in weights. That is, our suggested test statistics for spatial dependence are valid irrespective of whether the weights matrices are endogenous or not. We show the asymptotic properties of the suggested test statistics under the null and local alternative hypotheses. These test statistics are simple to calculate because their computations only require the least-squares type (OLS/GLS) estimates. We investigate the size and power properties of the robust tests through a Monte Carlo study. The results are in line with our theoretical findings and indicate that our robust tests have good size and power properties. Using a dual gravity model of international trade, we also illustrate the use of these tests in an empirical specification search.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the model specification which extends the SAR model considered in Qu and Lee (2015) to allow for spatial dependence in the disturbance term as well. Section 3 develops the ML estimation approach for our extended model. Section 4 presents the proposed test statistics along with some standard test statistics. Section 5 contains a Monte Carlo study to investigate the finite sample size and power properties of the test statistics. Section 6 discuses the empirical application. Finally, Section 7 concludes the paper. Some technical derivations and results are relegated to appendices.

div.head: A Dual Gravity Model
div.p: Behrens, Ertur, and Koch (2012) derive a gravity equation from the quantity-based version of the constant elasticity of substitution (CES) model by assuming that the unobservable price indices are implicit functions of trade flows. Conveniently, the solution yields an econometric specification that properly accounts for interdependence between trade flows.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we derived robust LM test statistics for the autoregressive parameters of the SARAR(1,1) model that has endogenous spatial weights matrices. These test statistics are robust to potential endogeneity in weights as well as to the parametric misspecification in the alternative model. These tests can be easily calculated since their computations only require simple estimations. Hence, our test statistics have a computational advantage 14

We also suggested a robust test statistic for testing endogeneity of weights matrices in the local presence of spatial autoregressive parameters. Results from our Monte Carlo study are in line with our theoretical results and indicate that the robust tests have good size and power properties. Our results also show that the conventional test statistics that are robust to only parametric misspecification have large size distortions in the presence of endogeneity in spatial weight matrices. We also analyzed the effects of distributional misspecification on the finite sample performance of the tests statistic. The findings showed that our tests can perform well in the case of distributional misspecification in the error terms. Finally, using a recent empirical application, we illustrated how these tests can be helpful in identifying the correct specification.

Before we end this section, we need to emphasize several possible extensions for future research. First, our results on the asymptotic properties of robust test statistics are general enough and therefore can be extended to linear or non-linear spatial panel data models. Second, our testing approach can be used to develop similar tests for the matrix exponential spatial specification suggested by LeSage and Pace (2007). Last, our test statistic can also be extended to the GMM framework by following Taşpınar, Doğan, and Bera (2017).
